newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries slightly lower at opening Friday.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries slightly lower at opening Friday.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities opened slightly lower Friday following a night of active trading overseas.

The long bond was down 2/32 at 95-13/32 to yield 6.86 percent. The Treasury will announce details of its $19.25 year bill auction on January 30 at 1430 EST/1930 GMT. No other data were scheduled for release.
"It's a quiet morning. The U.S. Treasury market is still the cheapest G-7 market in the world on a relative basis and seems to be getting cheaper every day," said a trader.
The trader said all of the flows have been peripheral of late, that is coming off of what was happening in the corporate, mortgage and foreign markets, not based on Treasury fundamentals.
"There's no news today and the market is still very afraid of the Employment Cost Index (due Tuesday), but there's not a lot of volume," he said.

The U.S. dollar remained strong in overnight trading, lending some support to Treasuries. At one point the dollar/yen rate rose to 120.15 -- a 47-month high -- before retreating back below 119 on rumors the Bank of Japan intervened to support its currency. The outlook remained bullish for the dollar, however.
Despite the strength of the dollar, the trader said he wasn't sure it was having that large of an effect on the Treasury market of late.
"The dollar's been on a one-directional head recently" and not playing that large a role in the Treasury market, he said.

"The dollar's not having as beneficial an impact as it had had in the past. Incrementally, it's probably not going to rise any further so this (the impact of the dollar's increase) may be about played out," said Charles Lieberman, director of financial research at Chase Securities Inc.

Lieberman said he expected to see a downward bias in bond prices Friday as an appreciation grows that the U.S. economy has a fair amount of momentum and fourth quarter results will probably prove to be quite strong.
"Until there's evidence of slowing, bonds will suffer," Lieberman said.

Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp., said the dollar's retreat from overnight highs also could negatively impact the market. She said the bond market hadn't benefitted from the dollar's rise during the past three trading sessions.

Stephansen said there also was a lot of nervousness ahead of next week's economic data, especially the ECI. Also due next Friday is fourth quarter Gross Domestic Product that could reveal that growth took place at a more than 3.0 percent pace.
Later this session four Federal Reserve bank presidents will appear at a colloquium in St. Louis. Fed Governor Laurence Meyer was scheduled to address an audience in Mexico this morning.

Economists said the Fed likely could remain out of the banking system during its usual midmorning intervention period Friday, but a small add was possible. Fed funds opened at 5 3/16 percent, near the Fed's target rate of 5.25 percent.
The two-year note was at 99-21/32, down 1/32 to yield 6.06 percent. The five-year was down 2/32 at 99-15/32 to yield 6.38 percent and the 10-year was down 1/32 at 99-10/32 to yield 6.60 percent.
Three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.03 percent. Six-month rates were up one basis point at 5.13 percent and year bill rates were also up one basis point at 5.31 percent.
